# [Title of analysis]

TradeSeq allows you to examine gene expression changes after inferring pseudotime with another package (the tradeSeq vignette literally starts from a slingshot object). It uses a negative binomial generalized additive model.

### save_plot()

This document displays all the figures I make, but I also want them saved to disk — both as `.png` and `.pdf`. I only need to provide the ggplot object, a filename (without extension), and optionally the width and height of the figure. You will not see saving of figures happening in this HTML output file, because I hid those chunks with `echo: false`.

The figures for my written report contain subfigures spread across multiple scripts. Since I want to assemble these panel figures via R code rather than by hand, `save_plot()` can also optionally save the plot object itself to disk as an .rds file, for a final script to later combine with `patchwork`. Set `figure` to the name the figure should carry in the report (e.g. `"SF1A"`) to trigger this; leave it `NULL` (the default) to just save the `.png`/`.pdf` as normal.

A live ggplot object carries its underlying data along with it — for plots built from large Seurat objects, this can balloon the saved file to gigabytes. To avoid this, `save_plot()` converts the object to a grob (a static, pre-rendered drawing, with no data attached) before saving it as `.rds`. This is controlled by the `grob` argument, and defaults to `TRUE`, since converting a small plot costs nothing but forgetting to convert a large one is expensive. Set `grob = FALSE` only if a later step specifically needs the original, live ggplot object rather than its rendered form.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-05-helper-save-plot
save_plot <- function(p, filename, width = 10, height = 6, 
                      figure = NULL, grob = TRUE) {
  ## Save image on disk as png and pdf
  p_image <- p + theme_quarto() # Add Quarto-specific theme
  file_png <- file.path(dir_fig, paste0(filename, ".png"))
  ggsave(file_png, p_image, width = width, height = height, dpi = 150)
  file_pdf <- file.path(dir_fig, paste0(filename, ".pdf"))
  ggsave(file_pdf, p_image, width = width, height = height, dpi = 150)
  
  ## Save the ggplot object on disk as an rds file 
  if (!is.null(figure)) {
    p_rds <- p + theme_manuscript() # Add manuscript-specific theme
    file_rds <- file.path(dir_man, paste0(figure, ".rds"))
    # Convert the object to a grob if needed
    if (grob) {
      p_rds <- ggplotGrob(p_rds)
    }
    # Save on disk
    saveRDS(p_rds, file_rds)
  }
}
```

### theme_quarto() and theme_manuscript()

I created my own themes to add to figures. `theme_quarto()` is used to add themes to figures as displayed in the Quarto document and saved to disk as `.pdf` or `.rds`. `theme_manuscript()` is used to add themes to figures as they will end up in the manuscript.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-06-helper-themes
theme_quarto <- function(legend_position = "none") {
  theme_classic() +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_blank(),
      legend.position = legend_position
    )
}

theme_manuscript <- function(base_size = 8, legend_position = "none",
                         axis_text_size = 6, tag_text_size = 14) {
  theme_classic(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_blank(),
      legend.position = legend_position,
      axis.text = element_text(size = axis_text_size),
      plot.tag = element_text(
        face = "bold", 
        size = tag_text_size, 
        hjust = 0, vjust = 0
        )
    )
}

```

### printable_results()

For each test I'll run with tradeSeq, I'll want to perform multiple tests and print the most interesting result of each test (significant adjusted p-value, sort descending by fold change). The function `print_test_table` works for the three test I'll run (`associationTest()`, `startVsEndTset()` and `patternTest()`) - all are a little different, so I needed to adjust the code a little for each one. startVsEndTest() provides results for all lineages seperately, so the argument `lineage` provides of which lineage one wants results. 

tradeSeq does not automatically adjust p-values, so I do that for each.

I want all results automatically saved on disk, but there is the option to turn this off

```{r}
#| label: chunk-xx-helper-printable-results

printable_results <- function(results, test = NULL, lineage = NULL,
                              save_csv = TRUE) {
  results <- results  |>
    rownames_to_column(var = "gene") |>
    mutate(p_adj = p.adjust(pvalue, method = "BH"))
  
  if(is.null(test)) {
    stop("You did not provide what test you ran")
  } else if (str_detect(test, regex("association", ignore_case = TRUE))) {
    results <- results |>
      filter(p_adj < 0.05) |>
      arrange(desc(meanLogFC))
  } else if (str_detect(test, regex("startVsEnd", ignore_case = TRUE))) {
    if (is.null(lineage)) {
      stop("You did not provide a lineage!")
    } else{
      # Adjust p-value per lineage
      results <- results |>
        mutate(
            across(
            starts_with("pvalue_lineage"), 
            ~ p.adjust(.x, method = "BH"), 
            .names = "adj_{.col}"
          )
        ) 
      # Then extract results of given lineage
      lineage <- as.character(lineage)
      results <- results |>
        select(ends_with(lineage)) |>
        # !!sym(paste0()) makes it work without hardcoding the lineage
        filter(!!sym(paste0("adj_pvalue_lineage", lineage)) < 0.05) |>
        arrange(!!sym(paste0("logFClineage", lineage)))
    } 
  } else if (str_detect(test, regex("pattern", ignore_case = TRUE))) {
    results <- results |>
      filter(p_adj < 0.05) |>
      arrange(desc(fcMedian))
  }
  
  # Save the results to disk as csv.
  if (save_csv) {
    # If startVsEndTest, add the lineage to the filename
    if (str_detect(test, regex("startVsEnd", ignore_case = TRUE))) {
      file_csv <- paste0("tradeseq_", test, "_lin", lineage, ".csv")
    } else {
      file_csv <- paste0("tradeseq_", test, ".csv")
    }
    file_csv <- file.path(dir_tab, file_csv)
    write_csv(results, file_csv)
  }
  
  results
}

```

## [Subsection as needed]

Open the sce with Slingshot results

```{r}
#| label: chunk-07-open-sce
file_rds <- file.path(dir_data, "sce_shortread_astros_slingshot.rds")
sce <- readRDS(file_rds)

# Extract what's needed for tradeSeq
pseudotime <- slingPseudotime(sce, na = FALSE)
cell_weights <- slingCurveWeights(sce)
counts <- counts(sce)
```

I will later use GO terms, which only works on SYMBOL genes. SYMBOL is the default in our seurat object, but we also have some EnsemblID genes. These should not be included in our tradeSeq test.

I also filtered on genes which are expressed in a minimum percentage of cells. I did this because fitGAM() requires a lot of computing time and resources, and reducing the number of genes reduces this.


```{r}
#| label: chunk-08-gene-selection
# Filter genes which are expressed in a minimum proportion of cells
expressed_in_cells <- rowSums(counts > 0)
expressed_in_cells_pt <- expressed_in_cells / ncol(sce) * 100
genes_keep <- rownames(sce)[expressed_in_cells_pt >= filter_min_pt]

# Filter genes with SYMBOL name
# Might not be the most straight-forward way, but I prefer using dplyr
genes_keep <- genes_keep |>
  as_tibble() |>
  filter(!str_detect(value, "ENSG")) |>
  pull(value)
length(genes_keep)

```

```{r}
#| label: chunk-extra-test-run
# For the test run, randomly select 500 genes
# Set seed so that I can compare multiple runs
set.seed(1234)
genes_keep <- sample(genes_keep, size = 500)
# Filename for test run:
file_rds <- file.path(dir_data, "sce_shortread_astros_tradeseq_test.rds")

# Print time to see how long it took
Sys.time()

```

```{r}
#| label: chunk-extra-test-run-2
#| eval: true
# Print time to see how long it took
Sys.time()

```

This is very computationally heavy; only run it if it has not yet been run before (i.e. if the file with the results is not yet stored on disk).

```{r}
#| label: chunk-09-run-fitgam
# Uncomment line below when not performing test_run
file_rds <- file.path(dir_data, "sce_shortread_astros_tradeseq.rds")
if(file.exists(file_rds)) {
  # If it already exists, just open from disk
  sce_tradeseq <- readRDS(file_rds)
} else {
  # Prepare parallel computing
  n_workers <- as.integer(Sys.getenv("SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK", unset = "1"))
  bp <- BiocParallel::MulticoreParam(workers = n_workers)
  
  # Run fitGAM()
  sce_tradeseq <- fitGAM(
    counts = counts,
    pseudotime = pseudotime,
    cellWeights = cell_weights,
    nknots = 6, # 6 knots balances flexibility and overfitting
    verbose = TRUE,
    genes = genes_keep,
    parallel = TRUE,
    BPPARAM = bp
  )
  
  # Save on disk. I'm doing so in this chunk within the conditional statemtn
  # so that it only saves when fitGAM() was actually ran
  saveRDS(sce_tradeseq, file_rds)
}

```

```{r}
#| label: chunk-extra-test-run-2
#| eval: true
# Print time to see how long it took
Sys.time()

```

# Statistical tests

```{r}
#| label: chunk-extra-load-test-result
#| eval: false

# I have not ran the actual results yet, but can open my test runs to check
# whether the tests work
 file_rds <- file.path(dir_data, "sce_shortread_astros_tradeseq_res0.4_test500genes_2workers.rds")
sce_tradeseq <- readRDS(file_rds)

```

Associationtest finds genes which have general associations with lineages. These are not yet gene-specific.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-xx-associaton-test
res_asso <- associationTest(sce_tradeseq)

printable_asso <- printable_results(res_asso, test = "association")
printable_asso
```

StartVsEndTest tests which genes go up/dowm from start to end per lineage. This is probably the most important one, as I actually get lineage specifics here.

I set threshold at log(2). This tests which genes have a fold change that is significantly higher than 2 or significantly lower than 1/2 within or between the lineages of interest - otherwise genes with low foldchanges might still get high p-values. The output still contains all genes, so I can still use it for GO-terms.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-xx-startvsend-test

res_svse <- startVsEndTest(sce_tradeseq, l2fc = log2(2), lineages = TRUE)

printable_lin1 <- printable_results(res_svse, test = "startvsend", lineage = 1)
printable_results_lin1
printable_results_lin2 <- printable_results(res_svse, test = "startvsend", lineage = 2)
printable_results_lin2
printable_results_lin3 <- printable_results(res_svse, test = "startvsend", lineage = 3)
printable_results_lin3

```

diffEndTest compares lineages and tests whether they end at different expression levels. Somewhat nice, but depends; it might just be testing different 'clusters'. There also is a function diffStartTest, but all trajectories start from the same point, so that does not have much use

```{r}
#| label: chunk-xx-diffend-test
# Do I want this one?
res_end <- diffEndTest(sce_tradeseq)
res_end

```

patternTest tests whether lineages follow different shapes.
Same l2fc reasoning as with StartVsEndTest()

```{r}
#| label: chunk-xx-pattern-test

res_pat <- patternTest(sce_tradeseq, l2fc = log2(2))

printable_pat <- printable_results(res_pat, test = "pattern")
printable_pat

```


Optionally: combining pattern test with diffEnd as done in the tradeseq vignette
